title: Mean Reversion
teaches: Mean reversion as we trade it: a swing trade against a short, unusually fast drop in a leader, bought on the turn and never on the falling price, with the stop a few cents under the flush low, the first sell a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, and the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the plan working.

walkthroughs.title: EQT, August 2011: a leader flush in a fear spike
steps: EQT, August 2011. A leader up 32% gets hit in a market sell-off: five straight down days, 25.2% gone.
The flush day drops on 2.0x volume and closes right on the rising 200-day. That's a level to lean on. We wait.
August 9 it climbs back over the flush close. Buy at market, 26.76. Stop a few cents under the low, 26.00.
Another flush under the low and you're out. Instead it closes near the high; 3R next day. Too soon to sell.

walkthroughs.title: KRYS, August 2023: an earnings flush with a level
steps: Sometimes the flush is the earnings report. KRYS, August 2023: a leader up 59% slides four days, 17.9%.
It's 12.6% under a rising 50-day but still 20% above its 200-day. An overreaction, on 4.0x volume. We wait.
Next morning it opens above the flush close. Buy at market, 109.13. Stop a few cents under the lows, 106.88.
That day it closes at 3R, and 5R prints two sessions later. Sell some into that push, trail the rest.

walkthroughs.title: ACMR, September 2020: the post-blow-off snapback
steps: Even a broken parabolic can snap back. ACMR, September 2020: up 79%, then 38.6% gone in three down days.
The flush comes on 3.5x volume, the heaviest on the chart. RSI(2) hits 0. Stretched as far as it gets. We wait.
September 9 it turns. Buy at market, 20.00. Stop a few cents under the lows, 19.29: 3.5%, so fewer shares.
It bounces back to its short-term average, 8.1R at best, then goes sideways. A snapback, not a new trend.

questions.q: A leader's been running for months, then gets hit hard and fast for a few days. In one line, what's the mean-reversion trade?
choices: A bounce after a short, fast drop
A breakout of a quiet, flat base
A hold for months in a leader
Buying any stock that's down a lot
questions.answer: A bounce after a short, fast drop
questions.why: A bounce after a short, fast drop. When a strong stock gets hit way harder and faster than normal, it ends up stretched far under its short averages. Stretched things snap back. We're trading that snapback, a swing of a few days back toward those averages. It's not a breakout and it's not a long hold. And it's not any stock that's down a lot. It's a leader that got flushed, because a trend has to exist before mean reversion can kick in.
questions.lesson_line: We trade the snapback after a leader gets flushed, not the drop itself.

wrong.A breakout of a quiet, flat base: That's a base breakout. This trade buys after a hard drop, not after weeks of quiet.
wrong.A hold for months in a leader: That's a trend hold. This trade swings back toward the short averages, so think days, not months.
wrong.Buying any stock that's down a lot: A big fall isn't enough. A stock that was already weak has nothing to snap back to. We want a leader that got flushed.

questions.simple: It's a short bounce trade after a strong stock drops way too fast, aiming for a snap back toward its short averages.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-016, the definition and hold length)

questions.q: We only buy this flush in a stock that was trending up before the drop.
questions.why: True. Mean reversion needs a trend to revert to. A leader that gets hit hard ends up stretched under its own rising averages. The buyers who missed it step back in. A stock that was already sliding has no trend pulling it back up. Its bounce is just a pause on the way down. So before you study the flush, look left and make sure it was running. And it has to be above its 200-day. Under it, we don't buy stocks, period.
questions.lesson_line: Look left first. No trend before the flush, no snapback after it.

But nobody knows if tomorrow opens lower and flushes again. Let the stock show you. If it turns up, you buy with a real low under you. If it flushes again, you didn't own it. questions.lesson_line: The stretch is the setup. The turn is the trigger.

wrong.No, RSI(2) must reach 0 first: A lower reading only adds stretch. What's missing is the turn, not a deeper number.
wrong.Yes, it's fully stretched now: Stretched is the setup, not the trigger. Moves like this often keep going after the signal.
wrong.Yes, it closed under the lower band: A close outside the band is a stretch, not a reversal. Bollinger calls it a continuation signal at first.

questions.story: The flush day just closed. A leader lost 38.6% in three down days and closed under its lower Bollinger band. Tomorrow could go either way.
questions.simple: No, because a stretched stock can flush again tomorrow, so you wait for it to turn up first.

deeper.counter: A close under the lower band after a steep slide looks like the bottom. StockCharts warns the RSI(2) signal can be early, because moves often continue after it. The stretch sets up the trade. The turn is what triggers it.

Yes, it is the strongest mark

questions.q: Is this the flush you've been waiting for?
choices: No, it isn't stretched yet
Yes, it broke the 50-day
Yes, the gap is the flush
No, it's under the 50-day now
questions.why: No. Two red days and a 3% gap on average volume is a normal dip for a leader. Nothing's stretched yet. Breaking the 50-day doesn't make it a flush either. A flush is the selling speeding up: hard days and a wide bar, often on a jump in volume. Right now the sellers are just getting started, and you'd be guessing where they stop. Put it on your radar. If it keeps falling into a level and then turns, that's a different story.
questions.lesson_line: Two red days is a dip. Wait for a real stretch.

wrong.Yes, it broke the 50-day: Breaking an average isn't a stretch. Two red days on normal volume is just a dip.
wrong.Yes, the gap is the flush: A 3% gap on average volume is a normal day for a leader. A flush is way bigger than normal.
wrong.No, it's under the 50-day now: Sitting under the 50-day isn't the problem. It just isn't stretched yet.

questions.story: A leader gaps down 3% on its second straight down day, on average volume. It closed above its 50-day yesterday and sits just under it now.
questions.simple: No, because two red days on normal volume is just a dip, not a stretch worth buying.

questions.q: Tomorrow it turns up. Take it or pass?
choices: Pass, there's no level to lean on
Take it, 8% in four sessions is plenty
Take it, but with a wider stop
Pass, a four-day slide is too long
questions.answer: Pass, there's no level to lean on

Buyers need a reason to step in at a price, and mid-range there isn't one. So the turn can easily fail and drift right back down. Mid-range, you're just guessing where the selling stops. No level, no trade.
questions.lesson_line: No level, no trade.

wrong.Take it, 8% in four sessions is plenty: A drop with nothing under it is just a drop. Its size doesn't give buyers a reason to show up there.
wrong.Pass, a four-day slide is too long: Four days is fine. The problem is where it stopped, not how long it took.
wrong.Take it, but with a wider stop: A wider stop doesn't create a level. It just makes a bad spot cost more.

questions.story: A leader falls 8% in four sessions, the last day a 2.3 ATR drop. It stops in the middle of a two-month range, far from its averages and any gap.
questions.simple: Pass, because it stopped mid-range with no level under it, so buyers have no reason to defend it there.

questions.q: You're back at the screen. What's the play?
choices: Skip it, over 4% past the trigger
Buy at market, widen the stop
Place a limit at 50.00 and wait
Buy fewer shares to keep the same risk
questions.answer: Skip it, over 4% past the trigger

Past 4%, the risk is too wide and the bounce has already paid the easy part. A limit back at 50.00 is hoping, not a trigger. Let this one go. Missing a trade costs nothing.
questions.lesson_line: A missed turn is a missed trade. Let it go.

wrong.Buy at market, widen the stop: The stop only moves up, never wider. And you'd still be chasing.
wrong.Place a limit at 50.00 and wait: That's hoping it comes back. Our entries are market orders on the trigger.
wrong.Buy fewer shares to keep the same risk: Fewer shares is what chasing costs inside 4%. At 4.8% there's no buy at all.

questions.story: The turn printed at 50.00 while you were in a meeting. You see 52.40 now, 4.8% higher.
questions.simple: Skip it, because 52.40 is 4.8% over the trigger and we never chase more than 4%.

questions.q: It gapped past 3R. What do you do at the open?
choices: Your call, sell some or hold it
Sell a third at the open, by rule
Sell the whole position at the open
Add more shares at the open
questions.answer: Your call, sell some or hold it
questions.why: Your call. 3R sits at 44.50 and it opened at 45.10, past it. A gap past a level isn't an automatic sell. Some days I'll sell part into a big gap. Other days the gap is the start of the 3-5-7 day push I want to sell into. Either way the rest stays on with its stop. And at this point the stop can come up to breakeven.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past a sell mark isn't an order. It's a choice.

wrong.Sell the whole position at the open: Selling everything throws away the push you came for. If you sell, you sell part.
wrong.Sell a third at the open, by rule: No rule makes you sell at a gap. Selling part is a judgment call.
wrong.Add more shares at the open: A gap past 3R is where you weigh selling, not where you buy more. Adding up here chases your own winner.

questions.story: You bought at 40.00 with the stop at 38.50. Three days in, you haven't sold any yet, and 3R is 44.50. The stock opens at 45.10.
questions.simple: It's your call, because a gap past 3R is never an automatic sell, and the rest rides with its stop.

deeper.trap: A gap past your sell mark tempts two mistakes. One is treating the gap as an order to sell. The other is selling everything because the gap feels too good to keep. Don't do either. Selling part at the open is a judgment, and the rest stays on with its stop.

questions.q: When does the rest go?
choices: On a close under the 9 EMA line
On the first red day after 5R
At the next big round number
The first trade under the 9 EMA
questions.answer: On a close under the 9 EMA line
questions.why: On a close under the 9 EMA. A fast mover trails the 9 EMA, a steadier one the 20 EMA. This one's been riding the 9, so that's its line. Sell on a close under it, not the first tick through it. Fast stocks wick under the line all day and close back above. The close is the stock telling you the trend changed. Until then, let it run. That's where the big R comes from.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the rest. Sell on a close under the line.

wrong.On the first red day after 5R: One red day isn't a trend change. The line is your exit, on a close.
wrong.At the next big round number: A round number is a guess at a target. The trail lets the trend tell you when it's done.
wrong.The first trade under the 9 EMA: Fast stocks wick under the line and close back above all the time. Wait for the close.

questions.story: You sold part into a push and more later. The snapback has turned into a fast trend riding its 9 EMA.
questions.simple: On a close under the 9 EMA, because that's a fast mover's line and the close says the trend changed.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, E52)
the setup's trims are held (D-013)

questions.q: First sell's done. What can the stop do now?
choices: Move up to breakeven
Move down to give it room
Widen it to the 20-day
Come off, the sell paid for it
questions.why: Move up to breakeven. Once you've sold some, you can raise the stop to your entry. The window is anywhere from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell. Now the worst case on the rest is a scratch, and a winner you already sold into can't turn into a loss. It's a may, not a must, because some names need room to chop. What the stop never does is go down or come off.
questions.lesson_line: After the first sell, the stop can go to breakeven. Never down.

wrong.Move down to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down.
wrong.Widen it to the 20-day: That's wider. The stop never widens.
wrong.Come off, the sell paid for it: Every position keeps a real stop order with the broker, even after a sell.

questions.story: You made your first sell, a third of the position. The rest still has the original stop under the flush low.
questions.simple: It can move up to breakeven, so the rest can't turn a winner into a loss.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, A4, D41)
the setup's trims are held (D-013)

questions.q: Your honest stop is 3.7% away. Tightening it to 2% so you can keep your usual size is fine.
questions.why: False. The stop goes where the chart says you're wrong, under the low. Pull it in to 2% and it sits inside normal noise, so a good trade stops you out for nothing. 3.7% is fine. I prefer 1-3%, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% I'll take. You just buy fewer shares so the dollars at risk stay the same. Stop first, size second.
questions.lesson_line: Never squeeze the stop to fit the size.
questions.simple: False, because the stop comes from the chart and the size comes from the stop, so a wider stop means fewer shares.

deeper.example: I prefer stops of 1 to 3% of the buy, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% I'll take. This one's 3.7%, so it's a trade. With the risk fixed, the wider stop just means fewer shares. Past 5%, I mostly wait for a tighter trigger. Pulling the stop in only to keep the old size gets it backwards.

questions.q: It looks ready again. Do you add?
choices: No, not on a dip like this
Yes, add half at 40.50 on the dip
Yes, add and move both stops up
No, add only after the first sell
questions.answer: No, not on a dip like this
questions.why: No. You bought the full size once, at one price, with one stop. A dip back near your entry isn't strength. Adding here raises your average and puts more money on a trade that hasn't proven anything yet. If the dip turns into a break of your stop, you now lose more than you planned. An add to a working winner on strength is rare, a feel call, never the plan. Let this one work.
questions.lesson_line: One entry, one stop. A dip that hasn't proven anything gets no more money.

wrong.Yes, add half at 40.50 on the dip: Adding on a dip raises your average and your risk, on a trade that hasn't proven anything.
wrong.Yes, add and move both stops up: Two pieces, two stops, and a trade you never planned. Not on a dip.
wrong.No, add only after the first sell: That makes an add part of the plan. It never is.

questions.story: You're in at 40.00 with the stop at 38.50. It bounces 1R, dips back to 40.50 and looks ready to go again.
questions.simple: No. It's a dip near your entry, not strength, and adding just puts more on an unproven trade.

questions.q: Fourth turn this week. Do you take it?
choices: No, 3 tries a week is the limit
Yes, each turn is a new trade
Yes, but at half size this time
No, a stop-out ends the setup
questions.answer: No, 3 tries a week is the limit
questions.why: No. Three tries a week on one stock, six a month, then you stop. Three stop-outs this week means the stock is telling you something. Maybe the selling isn't done. Maybe the setup just isn't working in this market. Keep paying for it and a good name becomes a big loss in pieces. Half size doesn't lift the cap. Next week, a new trigger is a new trade.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week on one name, then step away.

wrong.Yes, each turn is a new trade: Sure, it's a new trade. But the cap is 3 tries a week, and you've used them.
wrong.No, a stop-out ends the setup: A stop-out doesn't end the name. A new trigger is a new trade, inside the weekly cap.
wrong.Yes, but at half size this time: Half size doesn't lift the cap. Three tries a week is the limit.

questions.story: You were stopped out on the same name three times this week. A fourth turn prints on Friday.
questions.simple: No, because three tries a week on one stock is the limit, and you've used all three.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E56, B21)

questions.q: A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.
questions.why: True. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.

questions.q: Four exit plans for a flush bounce. Which one isn't how we manage it?
choices: All out on a move above the 5-day
Sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push
Trail what is left under the 9 EMA
Breakeven stop between 2R and 5R
questions.answer: All out on a move above the 5-day
questions.why: All out above the 5-day. That's Connors' exit for his RSI(2) system, as StockCharts tells it, and he runs it with no stop. We don't sell it all at once. The first sell's a judgment, often into a 3-5-7 day push. The stop can go to breakeven between 2R and 5R. What's left rides the 9 or 20 EMA. A flush bounce sometimes turns into a real trend, and selling everything at the 5-day throws that away.
questions.lesson_line: We sell in parts and trail the rest. Connors sells it all at the 5-day.

wrong.Breakeven stop between 2R and 5R: That's ours. The stop can come up to breakeven between 2R and 5R.
wrong.Sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push: That's ours. A 3, 5 or 7 day push is often the best spot for the first sell.
wrong.Trail what is left under the 9 EMA: That's ours. A fast mover trails the 9 EMA and sells on a close under it.

questions.simple: All out at the 5-day isn't ours, because we sell in parts and let the rest ride a trail.

questions.q: Oliver Kell buys a Reversal Extension after a stock gets flushed. Where's his first profit target?
choices: A retest of the 20 EMA
The 200-day average
The prior all-time high
A fixed 3R on every trade
questions.why: A retest of the 20 EMA. Kell's stop goes just under the low of the reversal bar. He's quick to take profits and raise stops, and his first target is the stock coming back up to the 20 EMA. That's a smart target for a snapback, because it's the average the stock got stretched away from. It's his rule, not ours. Our first sell is a judgment, often into a 3-5-7 day push.
questions.lesson_line: Know the other traders' rules, then trade ours.

wrong.The 200-day average: Kell names the retest of the 20 EMA. The 200-day can be a long way off after a flush.
wrong.The prior all-time high: Kell's first target is the 20 EMA, much closer than an old high.
wrong.A fixed 3R on every trade: Kell names the 20 EMA. And our own first sell isn't a fixed 3R either.

questions.simple: His first target is a retest of the 20 EMA, the average the stock got stretched away from.

questions.sentence: Stretch mark 4 is ___ or more straight down closes.
questions.why: 3. A down close means the stock finished below the prior day's close. Our mark 4 is 3 or more of them in a row. Stockbee notes that after 3 to 4 days of negative action a bounce is a likely outcome. The first or second down day is a skip, because a slow, controlled decline is not stretched enough. A mark measures the stretch. The trigger is still the turn.
questions.lesson_line: Count the down closes. Three or more ticks mark 4.
questions.simple: 3, because mark 4 starts at three straight down closes, and the first or second down day is a skip.

questions.q: Your first day closes right on the lows. What's that telling you?
choices: An early warning sign on the trade
A normal shakeout you can add on
Just a pause before the next leg up
A cue to widen the stop for room
questions.answer: An early warning sign on the trade
questions.why: It's an early warning. A real turn should follow through. Instead this one closed at 162.53, right on the lows and just over your stop. The buyers who showed up this morning were gone by the close. That's the first sign the flush wasn't the end. You don't add, and you don't give it room. Your stop at 162.24 is still the exit, and here it was hit the next session. This was ELF, and it was a broken trend off a parabolic top to begin with.
questions.lesson_line: A turn that closes weak on day one is the early warning.

wrong.A normal shakeout you can add on: Never add to a trade closing on its lows. A weak close is a warning, not an invitation.
wrong.A cue to widen the stop for room: The stop only moves up. A warning is a reason to respect it, not move it.
wrong.Just a pause before the next leg up: A real turn follows through. Closing on the lows on day one is the warning, not a pause.

questions.simple: It's an early warning, because a real turn follows through, and your stop still decides the exit.

rests on a proposed card criterion the owner has not ruled on

questions.q: Kullamagi buys a long bounce after a huge parabolic drop. How does he get in?
choices: Opening range high, green candle
The close of the flush day itself
A limit at the low of the day
A market buy right at the open
questions.why: The opening range high, or the first green 5-minute candle. If it doesn't rally out of the gate, he buys any range break to the upside. Every one of those waits for the bounce to start. That's the same idea as our turn: let the stock prove the sellers are done, then get in. His setup is bigger, though. He wants a parabolic short that already fell 50-60% or more in a few days.
questions.lesson_line: Let the bounce start, then buy it.

wrong.The close of the flush day itself: That buys the falling price. He waits for the bounce to start.
wrong.A limit at the low of the day: That tries to catch the exact low. He waits for price to break up instead.
wrong.A market buy right at the open: He doesn't buy the bell. He waits for the opening range high or the first green 5-minute candle.

questions.simple: He buys the opening range high or the first green 5-minute candle, once the bounce has started.

questions.q: A stock trades 800,000 shares a day. Your size works out to 12,000 shares, 1.5% of that. That's too many.
questions.why: True. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 12,000 is 1.5% of 800,000. Past 1%, you're a real chunk of the day's trading. If the flush comes back and you need out, your own selling pushes the price down on you. So cut the size until it's under 1% of the volume, or pass. The size has to fit the stock, not just your stop.
questions.lesson_line: Never own more than 1% of a stock's daily volume.
questions.simple: True, because 12,000 shares is 1.5% of the stock's daily volume, and we never own more than 1%.

questions.q: Six quiet days into the 20 EMA. What setup are you looking at?
choices: A moving-average pullback
A mean-reversion flush day
A gap-down oops reversal
An undercut and rally
questions.why: A moving-average pullback. Six quiet sessions, light volume, no day bigger than 1 ATR, into a rising 20 EMA. That's a stock resting, not panicking. A flush is the opposite: the selling speeds up and the bar gets huge, often on heavy volume. Both can bounce, but you trade them differently. Name the setup first, then use its plan.
questions.lesson_line: A drift is a pullback. A flush is a shock.

wrong.A mean-reversion flush day: A flush is a hard, fast day. Nothing here moved more than 1 ATR.
wrong.A gap-down oops reversal: An oops gaps under the prior day's low and takes back the prior close the same day. No gap here.
wrong.An undercut and rally: An undercut and rally dips under a visible level and reclaims it. This drift undercut nothing.

questions.story: A leader drifts lower for six sessions on light volume, into its rising 20 EMA. No day drops more than 1 ATR.
questions.simple: It's a moving-average pullback, because it drifted quietly into a rising line with no hard down day.

deeper.trap: A pullback to a rising 20 EMA looks like a dip to buy, and it can be. A level alone doesn't make it a flush, though. A flush also needs real stretch: wide bars and the selling speeding up, often on heavy volume. A slow, quiet drift isn't stretched.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike line about a neighbouring card

questions.q: Four gaps down in a row. Which setup is it?
choices: Parabolic long
Mean-reversion flush
Moving-average pullback
Undercut and rally
questions.why: Parabolic long. Four straight gap downs into a 45% fall is a multi-day burst, the mirror of a parabolic run up. Our leader flush is different. It's one hard flush day in a leader, with no multi-day burst of gaps. The shapes matter because each one has its own plan. And if it's a stock under its 200-day, it's a no either way. Only indexes and levered ETFs get bought down there.
questions.lesson_line: A burst of gaps is parabolic. One hard flush day is ours.

wrong.Mean-reversion flush: Our leader flush is one hard day with no multi-day burst. Four straight gaps is a burst.
wrong.Moving-average pullback: A pullback drifts on light volume. Four gaps and a 45% fall is no drift.
wrong.Undercut and rally: An undercut and rally follows an ordinary dip. Four straight gap downs aren't ordinary.

questions.story: A stock gaps down four days in a row. It ends 45% off its peak.
questions.simple: It's a parabolic long, because four straight gap downs make a multi-day burst, not a one-day flush.

deeper.trap: A huge fall tempts you to call it a flush. Count the days and the gaps instead. One hard flush day in a leader is ours. A multi-day burst of gap downs is the parabolic long.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion the owner has not ruled on (the parabolic long's thresholds may still be pending)

questions.q: Dip under support, back above by the close. Name the setup.
choices: An undercut and rally
A mean-reversion flush
A parabolic long setup
An oops reversal day
questions.why: An undercut and rally. An ordinary dip pokes under a level everyone can see and shakes out the weak hands. Then it closes back above it the same day. No big stretch, no volume needed. A flush needs a hard, fast drop first. A parabolic long is a multi-day burst of gaps. An oops needs a gap under the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Undercut a level and take it back the same day: that's an undercut and rally, not a flush.

wrong.A mean-reversion flush: A 3% dip on ordinary volume isn't a flush. A flush is the selling speeding up hard.
wrong.A parabolic long setup: A parabolic long is a multi-day burst of gap downs. This is one ordinary dip.
wrong.An oops reversal day: An oops gaps under the prior day's low. This dip had no gap.

questions.story: A leader dips 3% under a clear support level on ordinary volume, with no gap. It closes back above the level the same day.
questions.simple: It's an undercut and rally, because an ordinary dip broke a clear level for a moment and closed back above it.

deeper.trap: An undercut that reclaims a level the same day looks like a flush that turned. The difference is the drop before it. An undercut and rally follows an ordinary dip and needs no volume. A flush needs a real stretch first, not a slow, controlled decline.

questions.q: Flush or something else?
choices: An oops reversal
A mean-reversion flush
A moving-average pullback
A parabolic long
questions.why: An oops reversal. A calm pullback, then a gap under the prior day's low. The same day it climbs all the way back over the prior close. The gap shook people out and buyers took it right back. Nothing about it is stretched. A flush needs a hard, fast drop first. A parabolic long is days of gaps, not one.
questions.lesson_line: Calm pullback, gap under, reclaim the same day: oops.

wrong.A mean-reversion flush: A flush is a hard, fast drop, not a calm pullback.
wrong.A moving-average pullback: A moving-average pullback drifts to a rising line. This one gapped under the prior day's low and reclaimed the prior close.
wrong.A parabolic long: A parabolic long is a multi-day burst of gap downs. This is one gap in a calm pullback.

questions.story: A leader is 6% off its high after a calm pullback. It gaps under the prior day's low, then reclaims the prior close the same day.
questions.simple: It's an oops, because it gapped under the prior day's low and won back the prior close that day.

deeper.trap: The oops and the flush both turn up after a drop, so the turn alone doesn't name the setup. Look at what came before it. An oops follows an orderly pullback. A flush follows a hard, fast stretch. Name the setup first, then use its plan.

questions.q: Will you be a buyer when it turns?
choices: Pass, no leader's run behind it
Take it, above both averages
Pass, the flush is too big
Take it, four red days is plenty
questions.answer: Pass, no leader's run behind it
questions.why: Pass. There's no leader's run behind it. Up 15% off its low isn't a leader getting flushed. It's a stock rolling over from a top. Everything else looks right: above both averages, four red days, a hard flush. But this trade works because a strong trend snaps back. No trend, nothing to snap back to. This was META.
questions.lesson_line: No leader's run, no leader flush.

wrong.Take it, above both averages: Above the averages is fine. The missing piece is the run before the drop.
wrong.Pass, the flush is too big: A hard flush is what this trade wants. The problem is what came before it.
wrong.Take it, four red days is plenty: Four red days can be plenty. But a stock with no leader's run has nothing to snap back to.

questions.story: The flush day just closed. The stock was up 15% from its 63-day low before a four-day slide, a 2.1 ATR flush. It still sits above both averages.

questions.q: It turns up the next morning. How do you read this chart?
choices: A broken trend, not a stretch
Too small a run to be a leader
A moving-average pullback to buy
A stretched leader, ripe to bounce
questions.answer: A broken trend, not a stretch
questions.why: A broken trend, not a stretch. Eight straight red days right off a parabolic top, slicing through the 50-day, isn't a leader getting flushed. That's the top breaking. A flush is short and fast. This was a long slide that never found a floor. Every oversold sign was there, RSI(2) at 0 and a 3x volume flush. Those don't fix a broken trend. The turn day closed red, and the stop was hit the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Check the trend before you count oversold signs.

wrong.A moving-average pullback to buy: A pullback drifts on light volume to a rising line. This sliced through the 50-day into a 3x volume flush.
wrong.A stretched leader, ripe to bounce: Eight days through the 50-day off a parabolic top is a break. RSI(2) at 0 doesn't change that.
wrong.Too small a run to be a leader: The run was big, up 58%. The run wasn't the problem. The trend broke.

questions.story: The flush day just closed. A stock made a parabolic top, up 58%, then fell eight straight days, through its 50-day. The last was a 3x volume flush, 21% down in all, with RSI(2) at 0.
questions.simple: A broken trend, because eight red days through the 50-day right off a parabolic top is a break, not a stretch.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the oversold signs alone. Eight straight down days, a 3x volume flush and RSI(2) at 0 all shout oversold. But the slide went through the 50-day right after a parabolic top. That's a broken leader, not a stretched one. Check the trend before you count oversold signs.

questions.q: You're stopped out. What's next?
choices: Take the loss, rebuy on a trigger
Buy back at once, it's cheaper now
Widen the next stop to give it room
Write the stock off for good
questions.answer: Take the loss, rebuy on a trigger
questions.why: Take the loss, and only buy it again on a new trigger. A new low on heavier volume than the flush means the selling wasn't done. The market broke and took it down too. Your stop did exactly its job: a 2.8% loss, and that day it traded down to 296.28. If it builds a new low and turns again, that's a fresh trade with its own stop. Cheaper isn't a trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A planned loss. Buy it again only on a new trigger.

wrong.Widen the next stop to give it room: The next stop goes a few cents under the next low. Never wider for comfort.
wrong.Write the stock off for good: A stop-out doesn't ban the name. A new trigger is a new trade, inside 3 tries a week.
wrong.Buy back at once, it's cheaper now: Cheaper isn't a trigger. Wait for the setup to turn again.

questions.story: You buy the turn at 320.55 with the stop at 311.69. Two sessions later the market breaks. The stock makes a new low on heavier volume and stops you out.

The stock made a new low, 296.28, under the flush low, on heavier volume than the flush day. The selling wasn't done, and the stop got you out early.

questions.q: Your stop fills. Did you do something wrong?
choices: No, a planned loss at the stop
Yes, you should have held it
Yes, the stop was too tight here
No, so buy it back right away
questions.answer: No, a planned loss at the stop
questions.why: No. That's a planned loss, the trade working the way it's built. You risked 2.0% to find out if the turn was real. It wasn't. The index made a new low and dragged it down to 99.80. A wider stop would've been hit too, just for more money. This was SBUX in March 2025. A loss at the stop is the cost of being there for the ones that work.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out at your plan is a planned loss, not a mistake.

wrong.Yes, you should have held it: The stop is the exit. Holding past it turns a 2.0% loss into whatever the market gives you.
wrong.Yes, the stop was too tight here: It traded to 99.80, way under your stop. Any stop near the low got hit.
wrong.No, so buy it back right away: Not a mistake, but the trade's over. Buying now buys the falling price, not a turn.

questions.story: You buy at 105.48 with the stop at 103.39. Day one trades down to 99.80 and closes at 101.13, in the lower quarter of its range. The index makes a new low.
questions.simple: No, because a loss at your planned stop is the plan working, not a mistake.

questions.q: The turn prints tomorrow. What's your call?
choices: Pass, no level to lean on
Take it, 6x volume is a climax
Take it, 17.5% is a deep stretch
Pass, it's a report-day drop
questions.answer: Pass, no level to lean on
questions.why: Pass. There's nothing under it to lean on. It flushed hard on the report, 6x volume, but volume tells you how much got sold, not where buyers step in. A report drop with no level under it keeps falling. And the honest stop is 6.4% away. That's past the 5% I'll take, so I'd wait for a tighter trigger anyway. This was DASH in May 2024. The turn day reclaimed and failed.
questions.lesson_line: A report drop with nothing under it keeps falling.

wrong.Take it, 6x volume is a climax: Volume isn't a level. Without one under it, a report drop keeps falling.
wrong.Take it, 17.5% is a deep stretch: Depth isn't a level either. And a 6.4% stop is past what we take.
wrong.Pass, it's a report-day drop: A report flush alone isn't a skip. KRYS flushed on its report and worked. The missing level is the problem.

questions.story: The flush day just closed. A leader up 27% fell 17.5% in three days after its report, a 3.2 ATR flush on 6x volume. The honest stop is 6.4% away. Nothing sits under it.
questions.simple: Pass, because nothing sits under it to lean on, and the honest stop is wider than we take.

deeper.trap: 6x volume looks like the selling got done in one go. But volume says how much got sold, not where buyers step in. A flush wants to land on something: a prior breakout, a round number, a rising average, an open gap. DASH had the volume and the stretch, and its turn day reclaimed and failed.

questions.q: Two flushes today. Which one do you want?
choices: B: 4th day, a level, and fear
A: the calm market is safer
About the same, both are flushes
Neither, the fear is too high
questions.answer: B: 4th day, a level, and fear
questions.why: B. It's had four days to get stretched, it landed on a prior breakout level, and the whole market's scared. VIX at 31, breadth washed out. That's forced selling into a floor, the best version of this trade. A is a second red day in the middle of a range, with the VIX at 14 and the index at highs. Nothing's stretched, nothing's under it, and nobody's panicking.
questions.lesson_line: More stretch, a level and a scared market make the best flush.

wrong.A: the calm market is safer: Calm hurts this setup. A stock flushing alone in a calm market is telling you about itself.
wrong.About the same, both are flushes: They're not close. A is a normal dip mid-range. B has the stretch, the level and the fear.
wrong.Neither, the fear is too high: Fear is what this setup feeds on. A scared market is when good stocks get dumped with everything else.

questions.simple: B, because it's more stretched, it landed on a level, and the market's scared, which is when snapbacks work best.

deeper.trap: A calm market feels safer, so A can look like the better buy. For this setup it's the reverse. Fear in the whole market means good stocks get sold with everything else, and that's what snaps back.

questions.q: A leader flushed by a market-wide panic is a better bounce trade than one flushed by a guidance cut.
questions.why: True. A market panic dumps good companies with everything else. Nothing about the business changed, so buyers come back when the fear fades. A guidance cut is the company telling you its future just got worse. The bounce there is often a dead-cat bounce: it pops, then the selling picks up again. So ask why it fell before you ask how far.
questions.lesson_line: An overreaction is a setup. A broken business isn't.
questions.simple: True, because panic selling in a sound company snaps back, while a business that broke tends to bounce and keep falling.

deeper.trap: A broken business can still bounce, and that bounce can look like a turn. Bulkowski: once a dead-cat bounce completes, price resumes declining. So ask why it fell before you ask how far it fell.

questions.q: It looks stretched. Is this one you buy?

Take it, a 20% drop is a washout
Take it with a tight stop
Pass, wait for it to fall further
questions.why: Pass. A guidance cut and a fraud probe aren't an overreaction. They're a real change in the business. The people selling aren't panicking, they're repricing a company they no longer trust. That kind of drop gets a dead-cat bounce, a pop that fails and keeps falling. A tight stop just makes it a cheaper way to be wrong. Compare EQT in August 2011, flushed in a market sell-off with nothing wrong with the company.
questions.lesson_line: Judge why it fell, not just how far.

wrong.Take it with a tight stop: A tight stop can't fix a broken story. It just makes being wrong cheaper.
wrong.Take it, a 20% drop is a washout: The size isn't the issue. A broken business bounces, then keeps falling.
wrong.Pass, wait for it to fall further: A deeper fall doesn't fix the story. When the business changed, the bounce is a trap.

Same lesson for us: don't fade a strong trend. Let it show you it's tired first.

questions.q: It gapped right through your stop. What's the move?
choices: Sell the whole position now
Use 36.80 as the new stop
Hold and wait for the bounce back
Sell half, stop at 36.80
questions.why: Sell it all, now. Your risk was 40.00 down to 38.50. Double that and you're already past it at 36.80. The gap rule lets the first 30 minutes have a say, and their low becomes your new stop. But only while the loss stays inside 2R. Past that, there's no new stop. You just get out. A gap that big, still falling, isn't a shakeout. Don't let one trade wreck your month.
questions.lesson_line: Past 2R on the gap, get out.

wrong.Use 36.80 as the new stop: That only works inside 2R. At 36.80 you're past it, so there's no new stop.
wrong.Sell half, stop at 36.80: Past 2R the rule is out, not trim. No part of it stays.
wrong.Hold and wait for the bounce back: Holding past the ceiling is how a planned loss becomes a disaster.

questions.story: You bought at 40.00 with the stop at 38.50. The stock gaps down and the first 30 minutes make a low of 36.80, still falling.
questions.simple: Sell it all, because the first half hour took the loss past 2R, and past 2R you just get out.

deeper.trap: The gap rule has two branches, and the trap is using the friendly one. Inside 2R, the first 30-minute low becomes the new stop and the trade can live. Past 2R, there's no new stop. You get out. Measure the loss at the first 30-minute low before you decide which branch you're on.

Four red days into a hard flush, landing on its rising 50-day, a level buyers lean on. The turn printed. The report's two weeks out, well clear of the 3-day window. Buy at market. It dipped under the flush low before turning, so the stop goes a few cents under the turn day's low.
